title: Chance and Samples
summary: Populations and samples, parameters and statistics, and what makes a sample random.
hints: A parameter describes the whole population (Greek letters); a statistic describes a sample (Roman letters).
Random sampling doesn't guarantee a typical sample. It makes the size of chance errors predictable.
A seed fixes where R's random-number generator starts.

quiz.prompt: You survey 120 of a university's 9,000 doctoral students and find a mean stress score of 3.4. Which is the **statistic**?
choices: The mean stress of all 9,000 doctoral students
The mean of 3.4 in your 120 respondents
The 9,000 students
The stress questionnaire
quiz.explain: A **statistic** (x̄ = 3.4) describes the sample you measured. The mean of all 9,000 is the **parameter** (μ), which you don't know and want to estimate. The 9,000 are the population.

quiz.prompt: You roll a fair die 60 times. Which result is most likely?
choices: Exactly 10 sixes, every time you try it
Somewhere around 10 sixes, but rarely exactly 10
No sixes in the first five rolls means more sixes later
Exactly 1 six in every 6 rolls
quiz.explain: Probability is a **long-run proportion**: about 1/6 of rolls, give or take chance variation. A die has no memory, so a run without sixes doesn't make sixes "due" (the gambler's fallacy).

choices: A random sample always matches the population exactly
Random samples are always larger
Every member has a known chance of selection, so how far samples stray from the population by chance can be calculated
Randomness removes measurement error
quiz.explain: A random sample can still be unusual. What randomness buys is **predictable** chance error: its size can be worked out (the standard error), and every confidence interval and p-value rests on that. A convenience sample has no such guarantee.

choices: Makes R's random numbers truly random
Makes the next random draws come out the same every time the script is run
Draws 2,026 random numbers
Stops `sample()` from repeating values
quiz.explain: R's random numbers come from an algorithm. The seed fixes its starting point, so the same code gives the same draws, which makes a simulation or random assignment reproducible. (Use any number; just record it.)

quiz.prompt: You pick 10 participants from a list of 200 names. Should you sample with or without replacement?
choices: With replacement, so everyone has the same chance
Without replacement: nobody should be picked twice
It makes no difference
With replacement, because the list is short
quiz.explain: People can't take part twice, so draw without replacement: `sample(names, 10)`, R's default. With-replacement draws model processes that can repeat (die rolls) or populations so large that it doesn't matter, and they're the basis of bootstrapping.

quiz.prompt: The Crew Log holds essentially everyone who flew to space from 1961 to 2019. Is it a sample?
choices: Yes, a random sample of astronauts
No: for that period it's close to the whole population, so its means are parameters, not estimates
No, because it has more than 30 rows
Yes, because every dataset is a sample
quiz.explain: For "people who flew 1961–2019", the log is nearly the whole population: its median mission length simply *is* that group's median. Sampling from it, as you'll do in the Sampling Machine, shows what a researcher with only a sample would see. Inference Station takes up what a test means for a near-complete population.
